passages.title: Mapping the Dark
The Shortcut
passages.text:
The summer I turned sixteen, I took a job sweeping floors at Hanley & Daughters, a bookbindery that had operated on Water Street since 1934. The shop {{1|smelled of glue, leather, and old paper,}} and the radio on the workbench played the same baseball station all day. {{2|Mrs. Hanley was the owner, she}} had been binding books in that room for almost fifty years.

For the first few weeks, I only swept and watched. Mrs. Hanley folded large printed sheets into sections called signatures, sewed the signatures together along their spines, and {{3|then she glued}} each sewn block into a cover. Each of the hundreds of books on her shelves {{4|were}} sewn by hand. She never used the machine that sat in the corner, {{5|which she called "the shortcut."}}

In August, she finally let me bind a book of my own. My first attempt was a disaster. The stitches were uneven, the spine leaned to one side, and the cover {{6|wouldn't hardly}} close. I expected her to drop it in the scrap bin. {{7|Nevertheless,}} Mrs. Hanley studied it for a long time, turning it over in her hands, before she gave it back to me. "Now make one with {{8|less}} knots," she said.

I made eleven more books before school started again. {{9|}} Each one was a little better than the last. By the twelfth, the stitches were even, the spine was straight, and the cover closed {{10|flatly and evenly without any gaps.}} Mrs. Hanley put that book on the shelf beside her own, and it is still there today.

passages.title: The Town That Turned Down Its Lights
Mile Eighteen
passages.text:
Every April, about two hundred volunteers staff the water stations along the Harbor City Marathon. For the past three years, I {{1|have been}} one of them, and I have learned that handing a cup of water to a stranger who is running past is harder than it looks.

Our station sits at mile eighteen, the point where many runners begin to tire. Our captain, a retired nurse named Delia Moss, placed us in pairs in the narrow gap {{2|among}} two long tables and told us to hold each cup {{3|either by its base or to pinch it}} near the top. A cup held this way, she explained, leaves room for a runner's hand to close around {{4|it, a}} cup gripped by its rim is easily knocked away and tends to {{5|loose}} half its water.

[1] The first runners reached us at 9:40. [2] By noon our tables were sticky, our shoes were soaked, and we had handed out more than eleven thousand cups. [3] They were the elite athletes, moving so fast that most of them never slowed down. [4] Behind them came thousands of others, {{6|in various different kinds of conditions}}. {{7|}}

Around one o'clock, a runner in a faded green shirt stopped at our table, drank two cups, and {{8|asks}} whether she was still on pace to finish before the course closed. Delia checked her watch and told her yes, as long as she kept moving. The runner thanked Delia and {{9|I}} and set off again at a slow, steady jog.

I never learned whether she made it. {{10|Still,}} when the results were posted that evening, I caught myself scanning the list for a runner in a green shirt, which is not, it turns out, something a results list records.

passages.title: The Box That Changed Shipping
The Third Position
passages.text:
[1] By the early 1920s, the streets of Cleveland, Ohio, were crowded with automobiles, horse-drawn wagons, bicycles, and pedestrians, all competing for the same space. [2] Some intersections had signals, but most of these could show only two commands: stop and go. [3] Because the signal switched instantly from one to the other, {{1|drivers already in the middle of an intersection had no warning that cross traffic was about to start}}.

[4] Garrett Morgan, a Cleveland inventor and businessman, had seen the danger firsthand. [5] {{2|Already known for a safety hood that firefighters and rescuers wore in smoke-filled spaces, his attention turned}} to the problem of the intersection. [6] His solution was a signal with a third position. [7] Before switching between stop and go, the signal would halt traffic in {{3|every direction, this gave}} drivers in the intersection time to clear it.

[8] Morgan received a patent for his design in 1923. [9] The signal itself was a T-shaped pole with arms that a person turned by hand, {{4|and so it}} looked little like the electric lights used today. [10] {{5|However,}} its central idea, a pause between stop and go, survives in the yellow light that appears at nearly every modern intersection.

[11] {{6|Morgan reportedly sold the rights to his signal to the General Electric Company for $40,000.}} [12] The sum allowed him to expand his other businesses, which included a newspaper and a company that made hair-care products. [13] Morgan {{7|has continued}} to work on inventions for the rest of his life, though none became as widely known as the signal.

[14] Historians are careful to note that Morgan did not invent the traffic signal; {{8|several earlier designs}} existed before his. [15] What he contributed was a solution to a specific problem that the earlier {{9|signals'}} had created. [16] {{10|In this way, his work shows how an invention can matter not because it is the first of its kind but because it fixes a flaw in what came before.}}

passages.title: A Pan with a Hole in the Middle
Drawing the Future
Falling Into Place
passages.text:
[1] In 1984, Alexey Pajitnov was working as a researcher at a computer center of the Soviet Academy of Sciences in Moscow. [2] In his spare time, he wrote small programs to test what the center's computers could {{1|do, one}} of them became the most famous puzzle game in the world.

[3] The idea came from pentominoes, a puzzle in which players fit together shapes made of five squares. [4] Pajitnov simplified the shapes to four squares each and set them {{2|falling, so that players had to rotate}} them quickly into place. [5] When a horizontal row was completely filled, it vanished, {{3|and so, as a result, the}} pieces above it dropped down. [6] He named the game Tetris, combining "tetra," the Greek prefix for four, with "tennis," his favorite sport.

[7] The computer Pajitnov used could not display graphics, so the first version drew {{4|it's}} pieces with letters and brackets. [8] Even so, colleagues who tried the game {{5|found it difficult to stop playing.}} [9] Copies spread from machine to machine across Moscow{{6| and}} then beyond the Soviet Union. {{7|}}

[10] Because Pajitnov had written the game at a state institution, the rights to it belonged {{8|not to him, but to the government}}. [11] For years, he earned almost nothing from it. [12] {{9|Eventually, though,}} he moved to the United States and, in 1996, co-founded a company that controls the Tetris name.

passages.title: A Cloudy Solution
A Wallpaper Nobody Wanted
Side by Side
Every Man Home
passages.text:
[1] In August 1914, Ernest Shackleton's ship Endurance left England for Antarctica, where he hoped to lead the first crossing of the continent on foot. [2] In January 1915, the pack ice of the Weddell Sea closed around the {{1|ship, the crew}} could do nothing but wait. [3] For months the ice slowly squeezed the hull, and in November 1915 Endurance {{2|sunk}} beneath it.

[4] The twenty-eight men camped on the drifting ice for months. [5] When the ice began to break up in April 1916, they {{3|rowed three lifeboats to Elephant Island, a barren, uninhabited place}}. [6] Knowing that no ship would search such a remote spot, Shackleton and five companions sailed one lifeboat about 800 miles across stormy seas to South Georgia, {{4|which}} a whaling station operated.

[7] Because they had landed on the island's empty side, Shackleton and two others then {{5|hiked and walked}} across its unmapped mountains to reach the station. [8] It took four attempts, but in August 1916 Shackleton {{6|finally}} reached Elephant Island and rescued all twenty-two men waiting there. [9] Not one member of the crew {{7|were lost}}.

[10] In 2022, an expedition found the wreck of Endurance nearly 10,000 feet below the surface of the Weddell {{8|Sea; remarkably well}} preserved.

passages.title: Books on Horseback
passages.text:
[1] During the Great Depression, many families in the mountains of eastern Kentucky lived far from any library, and the roads that reached them were often little more than rocky creek beds. [2] In 1935, the Works Progress Administration (WPA), a federal agency that created jobs for the unemployed, began a program that brought books to these families in the only way {{1|possible; on horseback}}.

[3] The riders, most of {{2|them were women,}} were known as packhorse librarians. [4] Each rider followed a route that could cover many miles each week, carrying books and magazines in saddlebags to homes, one-room schools, and remote {{3|communities. Where}} no car could go. [5] {{4|Riding through rain and snow, the mountain trails were dangerous for the librarians.}} [6] When a trail grew too steep or muddy, the riders often {{5|have had to}} dismount and lead their horses or mules on foot.

[7] The books themselves posed a challenge. [8] The program had almost no money for buying materials, so nearly everything the librarians carried was donated, and much of it arrived worn or damaged. [9] {{6|However,}} the librarians did not throw these materials away. [10] They mended torn pages and pasted recipes, quilt patterns, and stories clipped from old magazines into handmade scrapbooks. {{7|}}

[11] For many families, a rider's visit was {{8|anticipated with eagerness and looked forward to}}. [12] Some readers asked for books about farming or health, and adults who had never learned to read sometimes asked their children {{9|to read aloud}} to them. [13] The program ended in 1943, when wartime jobs became plentiful and the WPA was shut down. [14] By then, the packhorse librarians had carried books to thousands of families who might otherwise have had almost none.

passages.title: A Tree for Boston
passages.text:
[1] On the morning of December 6, 1917, the harbor of Halifax, Nova Scotia, was crowded with ships supporting the war effort in Europe. [2] In a narrow passage of the harbor, the French cargo ship Mont-Blanc, {{1|which was loaded with explosives}} collided with a Norwegian vessel, the Imo. [3] The collision started a fire aboard the Mont-Blanc, and {{2|they}} quickly abandoned ship and rowed for the opposite shore. [4] Crowds gathered along the waterfront to watch the burning ship {{3|drift slowly and gradually}} toward a pier.

[5] At a nearby railyard, a train dispatcher named Vince Coleman learned of the danger. [6] {{4|Rather than flee, he}} stayed at his telegraph key and sent a warning to stop an incoming passenger train.

[7] At about 9:04 a.m., the Mont-Blanc exploded. [8] The blast, one of the largest explosions ever caused by people before the atomic age, flattened much of the city's north end. [9] The explosion and the fires that followed it {{5|was}} responsible for nearly 2,000 deaths, and thousands more people were injured. [10] Coleman was among those killed. [11] {{6|However,}} his warning is believed to have stopped the train and saved its passengers.

[12] News of the disaster spread quickly. [13] Within days, a relief train from Boston arrived carrying doctors, nurses, and supplies, {{7|in spite}} a blizzard that struck the region the day after the explosion. [14] To thank Boston, Nova Scotia sent a Christmas tree to the city the following year. [15] Since 1971, the province has sent a tree {{8|every year, it}} stands on Boston Common throughout the holiday season.

candidates.subskill: Evaluating whether an essay meets a goal
candidates.stem: Suppose the writer's primary purpose had been to explain how Central Park was designed to look natural. Would this essay accomplish that purpose?

choices.A: Yes, because it describes in detail how every tree in the park was chosen.
choices.B: No, because it treats the design briefly and turns to the park's human cost.
choices.C: Yes, because its main focus is the engineering of the sunken crosstown roads.
choices.D: No, because it never says that the park was designed rather than natural.

candidates.evidence: almost every hill and pond was designed
candidates.explanation: The essay mentions the designed landscape briefly but devotes much of its length to the displacement of Seneca Village, so it does not mainly explain the natural-looking design.

A.rationale: The essay does not describe how trees were chosen.

C.rationale: The roads are mentioned in one sentence.

D.rationale: Sentence 4 says almost every hill and pond was designed.

hints: How much of the essay is about the design?

strategy.explanation: Check the essay against the exact purpose.

candidates.remember: Judge the whole essay against the goal.
